title: One-way valve

brief.story: People keep plugging the battery in backwards and killing the LEDs. A diode in the feed lets current through one way only, so a reversed battery does nothing at all. It costs a little voltage.
brief.goal: Fit a diode between column 3 and column 8 so LED1 carries 18–20 mA.

hints: The diode goes from the + feed (column 3) to R1 (column 8). Current flows from its anode to the banded cathode.
Band towards the LED: anode in column 3, cathode in column 8. Backwards, it blocks everything.
With the diode the LED gets (9 − 0.7 − 2.0) ÷ 330 = 19.1 mA. A plain wire instead gives 21.2 mA: too much.

spec.explain: A silicon diode keeps about 0.7 V when it conducts, and blocks completely the other way round.

debrief: A diode is a one-way valve: forwards it conducts and keeps about 0.7 V for itself; backwards it blocks. In series with a supply it’s reverse-polarity protection: put the battery in wrong and nothing flows, so nothing breaks. The 0.7 V it costs is why the LED runs at 19 mA instead of 21.
